title: Kamarajar Visits the Soviet Union: Industrial Planning and Social Welfare (1966)
summary: In July 1966, Congress President K. Kamaraj toured the Soviet Union, assessing heavy industrial planning and state-funded education through the practical lens of rural upliftment.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 169: நேருவின் திருத்தம்: “நான் சொல்லவில்லை; அவர்கள் சொன்னார்கள்”
full_text:
In July 1966, Congress President K. Kamaraj embarked on a landmark official visit to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.

In Moscow, Soviet dignitaries rolled out the red carpet, touring Kamaraj through colossal steel foundries, automated tractor manufacturing plants, and advanced hydroelectric turbines. Eager to impress the Indian leader, Soviet officials inquired:
"Mr. Kamaraj, what do you think of our vast industrial capacity and engineering achievements?"

Kamaraj nodded appreciatively and replied with characteristic rural pragmatism:
"Your factories and heavy machines are truly impressive. But steel and concrete do not tell me how the common citizen lives. Take me to the places where ordinary factory workers eat lunch, and take me to the neighborhood schools where their children study!"

The surprised hosts arranged an immediate visit to municipal worker housing estates and primary schools in the Moscow suburbs. Kamaraj inspected the school kitchens, observed children eating hot, nutritious lunches provided free by the state, and noted that every child received comprehensive medical checkups.

Turning to his Indian delegation, Kamaraj remarked with deep satisfaction:
"You see! In this country, no child drops out of school due to hunger, and no laborer is ruined by medical debts. This is what we must achieve in our Indian villages! Industrialization is necessary, but the ultimate test of any government is whether the poorest child is fed, educated, and sheltered."

Kamaraj's observations during his Soviet tour reinforced his lifelong conviction that state-funded public education and child welfare are the bedrock of genuine social democracy.
